notes:
I had a limited number of searches and page reads, so some sites on your list don't appear below. I didn't reach bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or any of the denominational sites (ligonier, gty, seedbed, lcms and so on). Most of what follows comes from the commentaries collected on biblehub.com, studylight.org and blueletterbible.org, plus Enduring Word (David Guzik) and oca.org.

**Overview**
- Guzik's title is "No Compromise." He says the psalm shows David worrying more about the evil inside himself than the evil coming from others. He quotes Kidner that the Hebrew of the middle verses is hard, but the overall point is clear: a prayer against insincerity and compromise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: It is a prayer for deliverance from sins to which affliction tempted him, and from the enemies who caused it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-10.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: David's need was urgent, so he called on the LORD by name and asked for quick help. A parent hears the voice of a child's cry, not just the words, and God hears His people the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Spurgeon notes that the Psalmist was now in some distress, whereof he was deeply sensible, as is evident from the vehemency of his spirit, shown by his repeating the request. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps141.cfm
- Constable thinks David probably prayed this at the time of the evening offering (about 3 p.m.) and requested a speedy reply. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-2.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: incense smoke rises like prayer, pleases God like a sweet smell, and needs "fire," meaning fervent prayer (James 5:16). If David wrote this as a fugitive from Saul, prayer was standing in for temple worship he couldn't attend. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Matthew Henry makes the same point: David was now banished from God's court, and could not attend the sacrifice and incense, and therefore begs that his prayer might be instead of them. Clarke points out that the word used is *minchah*, an offering without blood, not *zebach*, an animal sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-2.html
- Calvin says the verse plainly alludes to the ceremonies of the law. God had appointed those symbols to assure His people that their prayers were acceptable, and David drew strength for his faith from them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-2.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the prayer should rise with the regularity of the incense, and with its acceptableness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-141.html
- Spurgeon reads the incense altar standing next to the altar of sacrifice as a picture of the perfect sacrifice and the all prevailing intercession of Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps141.cfm
- Maclaren calls it "the sacrifice of the empty-handed." Lifting empty hands admits our need and looks to God to fill them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/psalms-volume-2/the-incense-of-prayer.cfm
- Ellicott says the lifted hands are only a symbol of prayer, not an offering. Some link the incense to the morning sacrifice, so that the verse means prayer morning and evening, but he thinks this is hardly necessary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: David didn't want the mouth he prayed with to be used for lies or foolish talk. He quotes Kidner: "If the house of God needed its guards and doorkeepers, how much more the man of God!" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Bridgeway: people who are slandered, as David was, are tempted to answer with harsh and unwise words, and David prays that he may be kept from such sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-10.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik compares this to "lead us not into temptation" (Matthew 6:13). Avoiding the "delicacies" of the wicked means turning down the advantages that come with sin. He quotes Boice: David isn't too good for evil people; he is too much like them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Matthew Henry: we can be drawn in by any allurement or pushed by provocation, so we must pray about both. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_141.cfm
- In Clarke's outline, "eat of their dainties" means sharing in the feasts, teachings, false holiness, power, riches or honours of the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/psalms/141-10.html

**v. 5 (where readings really split)**
- **Traditional reading:** loving correction from a righteous person is like soothing oil. Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "When the ungodly smile upon us their flattery is cruel; when the righteous smite us their faithfulness is kind." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the last line as "their wickednesses." The healing oil will strengthen him to continue to pray for his enemies. Barnes reads it in a similar way: David won't sulk, but will still pray for those who rebuked him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-5.htm
- Matthew Henry says some take "the righteous" to mean God Himself, so David welcomes God's corrections as tokens of love. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_141.cfm
- Calvin (Reformed) agrees with most interpreters that David counted kind, gentle rebukes as the best ointment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-5.html
- **Ancient-version reading:** Clarke prefers the reading shared by the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint and other old versions: "Let the righteous chastise me in mercy, and instruct me: but let not the oil of the wicked anoint my head." He takes the oil as the flatterer's smooth talk. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-5.html
- Gill (labelled "Calvinist, Baptist" on StudyLight) mentions the Targum's reading, which takes the oil as David's royal anointing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-5.html
- Utley notes that The NRSV, TEV, NJB, and REB follow the LXX. His advice is to grasp the general sense and move on. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/psalms-141.html
- **Orthodox:** the OCA Vespers text uses the "oil of the wicked" reading. https://www.oca.org/files/PDF/Music/Rubrics/Horologion/office-vespers.pdf
- **Note on traditions:** the split here is about text and translation, not denomination. I found no evidence that Baptist, Reformed, Methodist or other Protestant traditions read this verse differently from each other.

**v. 6**
- Guzik says the Hebrew is very hard. He quotes Horne, who said he couldn't make sense of the verse, and suggests David may have meant Saul without naming him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Barnes takes the "judges" as Saul and his officers. Once they fall, the people will welcome David's fair rule. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/141-6.html
- Pulpit Commentary: Calamity opens the heart to receive instruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-6.html
- Gill and Benson read the verse as David sparing Saul at the rocks of En-gedi. The judges were "let go," and they heard his kind words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-6.htm
- The Geneva Bible says the people who followed wicked rulers will repent and turn to God, when they see their wicked rulers punished. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-6.htm
- Ellicott thinks "how sweet" is ironic: the defeated party will hear a victory song, not a party invitation. https://biblehub.com/psalms/141-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes and Spurgeon see David's followers as scattered like wood chips, with God's cause apparently at death's door. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-7.htm
- Delitzsch and Hengstenberg see hope in the image: ploughing breaks the ground so that new life can grow. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-7.html
- Kretzmann's commentary takes the same hopeful line: believers laid out at death's door will rise again like seed from prepared soil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/psalms-141.html
- **Textual question:** some Septuagint manuscripts and the Syriac read "their bones," meaning the executed judges. Ellicott keeps "our bones" as the harder reading. Cambridge thinks "their bones" is probably a later correction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-7.htm
- Clarke mentions a possible link to the massacre of the priests at Nob, translating "at the command of Saul." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-6.html

**v. 8**
- Calvin: praying in such a state is like the torn pieces of a body crying out to God, which shows the heroical courage of David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-8.html
- "Destitute" literally means "pour not out my soul," that is, don't spill my life (compare Isaiah 53:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-8.htm
- Benson thinks David means both bodily danger and sin, but chiefly the latter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-8.htm
- Guzik links the verse to 1 Samuel 26:19: David's enemies tried to push him toward other gods, but he took refuge in the LORD alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry: however cleverly a trap is set, God can protect His people from it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_141.cfm
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary applies the verse to Christians asking God to rescue them from the snares of Satan, and of all the workers of iniquity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-10.htm

**v. 10**
- Clarke: those who set traps usually fall into them themselves ("harm watch, harm catch"). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/141-10.html
- BibleHub's study notes say David leaves justice to God instead of taking revenge (Romans 12:19). Examples include Haman and Daniel's accusers. https://biblehub.com/psalms/141-10.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner on the "buoyancy" of the last line, from a man who has slipped through many nets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- Kretzmann applies the verse to the final rescue of believers into eternal life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/psalms-141.html

**Other views**
- **Orthodox:** Psalm 141 is always sung at Vespers. During this psalm the evening incense is offered. https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-daily-cycles-of-prayer/vespers
  - Fr. Lawrence Farley says the incense reminds worshippers that through Christ their worship is acceptable to the Father. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/appreciating-vespers
  - The verses are also sung at the Presanctified Liturgies in Lent. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-jillions/september-9-2014
  - Guzik, citing Trapp, notes that Chrysostom already knew this psalm as part of the Greek evening service. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-141/
- **Catholic:** I found no Catholic commentary. The only evidence is the Vulgate's "oil of the sinner" reading of v. 5 (see above) and the NAB translation listed on biblehub. https://biblehub.com/psalms/141-5.htm
- **Modern/critical scholarship:** the Cambridge Bible says it seems impossible to explain vv. 6–7 satisfactorily in their present place, and the poor link to v. 8 is an additional reason for thinking that these verses are misplaced. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/141-8.htm
- **Prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace:** I found nothing about this psalm from these movements.
